message.content:
In Texas, tenants have a number of statutory rights designed to protect them from unfair treatment and to ensure they receive a safe, habitable living environment. Below is an overview of key tenant rights under Texas law (Texas Property Code, Chapter 24) and related statutes: | Category | Key Rights | Practical Implications | |----------|------------|------------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge a security deposit up to **one month’s rent** for a residential lease.
• Landlord must return the deposit within **30 days** after the tenant vacates, unless the landlord provides a written itemized list of deductions. | • Keep records of the deposit amount and any receipts.
• If you move out early, you may still be responsible for rent until the end of the lease term unless the landlord finds a new tenant. | | **Habitability & Repairs** | • Landlord must maintain the premises in a **safe and habitable condition**.
• Must repair major structural defects, plumbing, heating, electrical, and other essential services.
• Must keep the premises free of pests and mold. | • Report problems in writing (email or letter).
• If the landlord fails to repair, you may withhold rent, pay for repairs and deduct from rent, or terminate the lease (see below). | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Tenant has the right to use the premises without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • Landlord cannot enter the premises except for emergencies, inspections, or repairs with proper notice (see next). | | **Notice Requirements** | • For non‑renewal or termination of a month‑to‑month lease, the landlord must give **30 days’ written notice**.
• For a fixed‑term lease, the landlord must give **30 days’ notice** if the lease is not renewed.
• For entry, the landlord must give **24 hours’ written notice** (unless emergency). | • Keep copies of all notices.
• If the landlord gives less notice, you may be entitled to compensation. | | **Rent Increases** | • Landlord may increase rent at the end of a lease term or with a 30‑day notice for month‑to‑month leases.
• No rent increase is allowed during the lease term unless the lease allows it. | • Review your lease for any rent‑increase clauses. | | **Lease Termination & Eviction** | • Landlord may evict for non‑payment of rent, violation of lease terms, or illegal activity.
• Landlord must serve a **3‑day notice** for non‑payment of rent (or 30 days for month‑to‑month).
• For lease violations, the landlord must give a **10‑day notice** to cure the violation.
• For illegal activity, the landlord may serve a **3‑day notice** to quit.
• After the notice period, the landlord must file an eviction action in court. | • If you receive a notice, respond promptly.
• You may contest the eviction in court. | | **Discrimination Protections** | • Under the Texas Fair Housing Act and federal Fair Housing Act, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected classes. | • Report discrimination to the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. | | **Right to Repair & Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect, the tenant may pay for the repair and deduct the cost from rent, or terminate the lease. | • Keep receipts and document the defect. | | **Right to Retain Security Deposit** | • Landlord may retain the deposit only for legitimate reasons (unpaid rent, damages beyond normal wear, etc.). | • If the landlord retains the deposit without justification, you can sue for the deposit plus damages. | | **Right to Access Records** | • Tenant can request copies of the lease, security deposit receipts, and any notices. | • Keep copies of all documents. | | **Right to Sublet** | • Tenants may sublet or assign the lease only with the landlord’s written consent (unless the lease prohibits it). | • Obtain written permission before subletting. | ### How to Protect Your Rights 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Understand the terms, notice periods, and any clauses that might affect your rights. 2. **Document Everything** – Keep written records of all communications with the landlord, including emails, texts, and letters. 3. **Report Problems Promptly** – Send a written notice of any maintenance issue and keep a copy. 4. **Know the Notice Periods** – If you receive a notice, verify that it meets the statutory requirements. 5. **Seek Legal Advice** – If you’re facing eviction or a dispute over the security deposit, consult a tenant‑rights attorney or a local legal aid organization. ### Resources - **Texas Property Code, Chapter 24** – The statutory framework for residential leases. - **Texas Commission on Human Rights** – Handles discrimination complaints. - **Legal Aid of North Texas** – Provides free legal assistance to low‑income residents. - **Texas Attorney General’s Office** – Offers consumer protection resources. If you have a specific situation (e.g., a notice you received, a maintenance issue, or a dispute over your deposit), let me know and I can help you draft a formal letter or outline the next steps.
